vignette:
Carla, a 37-year-old hotel manager of Latin American descent, had always prided herself on her resilience and capacity to handle challenges. However, ever since that night months ago, when she was assaulted by a colleague at a company retreat, life had transformed into a labyrinth of fear and confusion. The event replayed in her mind, not like a coherent narrative but as fragmented images that left her feeling paralyzed. She remembered the moment vividly-the laughter of friends, the feeling of safety, and then the abrupt shift to terror as she found herself cornered, her body betraying her with a sense of impending doom. Even now, when she attempted to articulate what had transpired, words eluded her, as if the very act of recalling it was insurmountable. This inability to find a coherent story left Carla grappling with intense shame, believing that somehow, she should have been able to prevent it; perhaps it was because of the kind of person she was that she had found herself in that situation. The belief that she was fundamentally flawed made the memories of the assault more accessible, as if they were waiting to confirm her worst fears about herself.

In the wake of the assault, Carla's negative appraisals of herself became a relentless cycle. She felt as if there was something fundamentally wrong with her, as though her body had become an enemy that continued to react with alarm even in safe environments. This constant sense of defectiveness pushed Carla to work excessively, convincing herself that if she just kept busy, she could prove to herself that she was strong and capable, rather than the flawed person she believed herself to be. Her belief that she was fundamentally broken led her to think that overworking was the only means of coping with her feelings, reinforcing her negative self-image each time she avoided confronting her emotions. Believing she was fundamentally broken, she felt that engaging in work was the only way to distract herself from the painful truth of her perceived inadequacies, driving her to fill every moment with tasks to stave off feelings of worthlessness. This incessant threat perception influenced her decisions profoundly. Each time a vivid memory of that night emerged, she felt compelled to bury herself deeper in work, convinced that focusing on tasks would shield her from the painful emotions tied to those recollections. Each time she resorted to excessive work to cope, it deepened her conviction that she was incapable of handling her feelings, further entrenching her negative appraisals of self-worth. Believing she was fundamentally broken, she felt that engaging in work was the only way to distract herself from the painful truth of her perceived inadequacies, reinforcing her negative self-image each time she avoided confronting her emotions. To cope, she began to overwork herself, filling her hours with back-to-back meetings and endless tasks. By immersing herself in her job, she believed she could keep at bay the haunting thoughts that would emerge whenever she was alone. Yet this strategy only served to intensify the memories; the more she avoided confronting her feelings, the more vivid and intrusive the recollections of that night became, as if they were waiting for her to slow down before crashing back into her consciousness. By avoiding the memories through her work, she inadvertently kept them alive and fresh, making them surge back more powerfully whenever she allowed herself a moment of stillness. She had learned that staying busy was the only way to keep the memories at bay, yet each time she returned to work, the effort to suppress the thoughts only made them more pronounced, as if they were waiting for her to pause before flooding back. She noticed that her attempts to avoid the memories only made them feel more immediate; the more she buried herself in work, the louder the memories became, as if her avoidance had inadvertently kept them fresh and unresolved. Yet, this strategy only deepened her sense of defectiveness; she often ruminated on how she could get revenge against her assailant, thoughts that spiraled into a dark obsession. Each time she engaged in this avoidance tactic by overworking, she felt even more convinced that she was incapable of managing her feelings, further entrenching her negative appraisals of self-worth. Each time she indulged in these fantasies, she felt a fleeting sense of power, but ultimately, it left her feeling even more defeated.

The memories of that night were ever-present, cropping up at the most unexpected moments, like when she saw coworkers laughing together, reminding her of the camaraderie that had been shattered. These intrusive memories often drove her to bury herself in work, as she had learned that keeping busy was the only way to suppress the emotional turmoil linked to those recollections. These intrusive memories often prompted her to withdraw into her work, as she had learned that keeping busy would help her suppress the onslaught of emotions linked to those recollections, reinforcing her decision to avoid confronting her trauma. These intrusive memories would strike when she least expected, leading her to retreat further into her work, as if burying herself in tasks could shield her from the emotional turmoil they ignited. Whenever Carla encountered people who bore even a passing resemblance to her assailant, her heart raced, and her stomach twisted in knots. She often found herself avoiding their company, fearing that any confrontation would trigger those painful recollections. Yet, in her attempts to evade these memories, she only exacerbated her dissatisfaction with herself, reinforcing the belief that she was somehow responsible for what had occurred. The shame she felt was compounded by the knowledge that she could not articulate what had happened or why she had been targeted. This silence about the trauma only reinforced her belief that she was weak, as the avoidance of discussing the assault prevented her from processing it, allowing the memories to linger and amplify. The avoidance of discussing the assault only reinforced her belief that she must be weak, as she couldn't bear to face the memories, leading her to feel even more inadequate when she realized how deeply those thoughts had taken root within her. This silence, combined with the avoidance of similar people, led to an insidious isolation that further entrenched her feelings of worthlessness.

Carla's strategies for coping were paradoxically detrimental. While she sought to distract herself through busyness, this very avoidance made the memories of the trauma more vivid and intrusive, as if they were waiting for her to slow down before crashing back into her consciousness. The more she worked to keep busy, the more her mind would betray her with snapshots of that night, leaving her feeling trapped between her desire to forget and the inescapable reality of what had happened. Her attempts to avoid the memories through overworking only intensified their vividness, as if all the suppression had kept them alive and unresolved, waiting for her to stop long enough for them to resurface. Each ruminative thought on revenge only served to deepen her conviction that she was a defective person, someone deserving of the pain she experienced.

Recently, Carla had begun to notice the toll this cycle was taking on her relationship with her partner. She found herself withdrawing, unable to share her burdens or allow him to help her. The shame and fear kept her isolated, and she realized she was building walls that threatened to destroy the connection she cherished. It was this awareness that finally compelled her to seek help. Sitting in the therapist's office, she felt a mix of hope and apprehension. She knew she couldn't continue living in this torment, but what frightened her most was the thought of having to confront the memories she had tried to bury. She longed to reclaim her life, yet the shadows of that night loomed large, whispering that she might never escape the darkness within. Each time she found herself turning to work to cope, it reinforced her belief that she was incapable of managing her feelings on her own, further entrenching her negative self-image as someone weak and fragile.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette does not convey how negative appraisals influence Carla's maladaptive strategies, missing the causal connection between her negative beliefs and her choices to cope.
  e.g. "If she had concluded that the world was dangerous and she was defenceless, staying home wasn't avoidance — it was the only rational thing to do."
  e.g. "The belief that speaking about it would make things worse kept her silent in her sessions, offering fragments instead of the whole picture."
  e.g. "Having decided that her feelings couldn't be trusted, she worked hard to stay numb — and had become quite good at it."

  e.g. "She had learned that if she kept the television on loud enough, the thoughts couldn't get a foothold — silence was the enemy."
  e.g. "After the memory surfaced during sex, she began finding quiet reasons to avoid intimacy altogether, telling herself she was simply tired or stressed."
  e.g. "To stop the images coming at night, she started staying up later and later, until exhaustion was the only reliable way to fall asleep."

  e.g. "Three years of avoiding it had told her something she couldn't easily argue with: that she must be more fragile than other people, or she would have been over this by now."
  e.g. "Each time she used a safety behaviour to get through the day, she felt the quiet accumulation of evidence that she couldn't cope without it."
  e.g. "The fact that she still needed to do all of this — the checking, the planning, the long way round — confirmed, in some wordless way, that she wasn't getting better."
